evidence: createApp() builds InMemoryUserRepository, InMemoryProjectRepository, InMemoryTaskRepository and UuidGenerator and injects them into UserService and TaskManagementService. This is composition-root wiring, which belongs in infrastructure.
Route handlers such as app.post("/projects/:projectId/tasks") only take fields from req.body or req.params and call service.addTask(...). The business behaviour lives in the application layer.
The error middleware maps ValidationError to 400, NotFoundError to 404, ConflictError to 409 and SyntaxError to 400. This is HTTP error translation, a transport concern.
PUT /tasks/:taskId/assignee checks `typeof assigneeId !== "string" || assigneeId === ""`. This is request-shape validation at the transport boundary, not a domain rule.
str() is a helper that coerces query-string values to strings, which is transport parsing.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/infrastructure/app.ts is the Express HTTP adapter and composition root. Everything it does belongs in infrastructure: it wires the in-memory repositories and the UUID generator into the application services, registers routes, reads request bodies, params and query strings, maps domain error types to HTTP status codes, and serialises JSON responses. All business work (creating users and projects, adding, listing, assigning and completing tasks) is handed to UserService and TaskManagementService. The only check in a handler is in the PUT /tasks/:taskId/assignee route, which requires assigneeId to be a non-empty string. That is a check on the request's shape at the transport boundary, not a domain rule. The str() helper only coerces query values. I found no persistence or domain logic placed in this file.
